activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Sofia went to the library with Grandma. There was a shape rug by the bookshelf. It had a red circle and a blue square.

Sofia wanted to build a tower. She put a circle block on top. The circle block rolled away. It rolled under the chair. "Why did it roll?" Sofia asked. Grandma picked up the block. "The circle is round," she said. "Round things roll."

So Sofia tried a square block. The square had flat sides. It sat still. She put a triangle on top. It sat still too. She put a rectangle on the bottom. The tower stood up tall.

A little boy watched her. He clapped his hands. "Do it again!" he said. Sofia gave him a square block. He put it on the tower.

Then they sang a little song. "Round ones roll, flat ones stay," they sang. One of Sofia's shoes was loose. She sat down and pulled it tight. Then she put one more block on top, very slowly, and the tower stayed.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Eleanor sat at the dinner table. She wanted a cookie for dessert. "Cookies are for later," said Mom. "Now we eat dinner." Eleanor looked at her peas. She ate one spoonful. Then she ate another.

"After dinner, will it be tomorrow?" asked Eleanor. Mom shook her head. "Tomorrow comes after a whole sleep," said Mom. Eleanor thought about that. Yesterday she had slept. Yesterday she had played in the rain. Today was a new day, and today she had peas.

Eleanor kept eating. She took her time. One pea, then another. She did not rush. Mom folded her napkin and waited. Dad folded his napkin too. The table was quiet and warm.

At last the bowl was empty. Eleanor held it up. "All gone!" she said. "Is it later now?" Mom smiled. "Yes. It is later now." Mom put one cookie on the table. Eleanor took a big bite.

"I know why I got the cookie," said Eleanor. "I ate my peas first. The cookie came after." Mom nodded. Eleanor looked out the window. "Tomorrow I will eat my peas too. Then tomorrow will be a cookie day." She patted her full tummy. "But now it is now, and I have my cookie."

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Madeline went to the park with Papa. She wanted to fold a green boat. But green paper was all gone at home.

"I have yellow paper," said Papa. "I have blue paper too."

Madeline sat on the swing. Papa pushed her high. She went up, up, up. Then she came down and got to work.

She took the yellow paper. She rubbed her blue chalk all over it. One, two, three strokes. Then more. The yellow turned funny. She looked close. It was green!

"Blue on yellow makes green," said Madeline.

She folded the paper. Fold, fold, fold. The boat had a pointy top. It was a green boat at last.

Now she needed water. The park had a little puddle by the slide. Madeline carried her boat over. She set it down. The boat floated!

"Look, Papa, look!" she said.

Papa clapped. Then Madeline made another one. Yellow paper, blue chalk. One, two, three strokes. Green again! Blue on yellow makes green.

She folded the second boat too. Two green boats sat on the puddle. They bumped side to side.

"Hello, boats!" said Madeline. She waved her hand up high.

"Why does the ball jump off?" he asked himself. "Because I throw too hard." So Rowan did not throw this time. He saw Ben near the hoop. Ben had his hands up. Rowan passed the ball soft and low. Ben caught it. Ben put it in the hoop. Swish.

story:
Alexander dug little holes in the dirt. He dropped a seed in each hole. Then he patted the dirt down, pat, pat. The sun felt warm on his hat.

He planted two rows of seeds. He watered the first row with his small blue can. Then he heard his swing creak in the wind. He ran to the swing and swung high, back and forth. He forgot to water the second row.

Every morning Alexander looked at his garden. Little green leaves came up in the first row. Tiny leaves, like baby hands. The second row stayed bare and brown. "Oh," said Alexander. "My seeds grew because I gave them water." So he got the can and watered the second row too.

Soon leaves came up there also. Alexander licked a drip of water off his tongue and smiled. Then a fat worm popped out of the dirt, waving hello.

Then the dog stopped. The boy sat down on the grass. He looked sad. A tear rolled down his cheek. Alexis peeked out from the tree.

Alexis walked over slowly. He smiled a big smile. "Hi," he said. "Want to see the ducks?" The boy looked up. He saw Alexis smiling. Then he smiled too. They counted the ducks together. "One, two, three, four!"

Later they sat on a bench. Alexis's mom gave them a plate with crackers. The boys shared every cracker.

"Smiling made you happy," Alexis said. The boy nodded. Then they both giggled, loud like the ducks.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
William sat on the clean bench in the backyard. He had a little seed in his hand. "What can I do with my seed?" he asked. "You can plant it," said Grandma.

William dug a small hole. He put the seed in. He patted the dirt down. Now he had to wait.

While he waited, he used his ears. He heard a bird sing. Then he used his eyes. He saw the bird hop. His nose smelled the flowers. His tongue tasted cold water. His fingers felt the soft dirt.

"Five senses," said William. "Ears, eyes, nose, tongue, fingers."

Days went by. Then a green sprout came up. It grew because the seed had water and sun. William sat and watched it grow a little more each day.

"Hello, little sprout," he said. "I will wait for you."

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Jake sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. His tummy felt funny. Today he would get a shot. He did not want a shot.

Mom held his hand. "A shot takes one second," she said. "Let's count it. One, two, three, done!" The nurse came in with a small tray. She had a cute bandage with a yellow duck on it. She put it next to a little fork-shaped pin, a toy prize for brave kids.

"My arm is tight," Jake said. He squeezed it into a ball. The nurse shook her head. "A tight arm hurts more. A soft arm hurts less." Jake let his arm go soft, like a sleepy cat. He asked, "Will it hurt a lot?" Mom said, "A tiny poke, then we get ice cream."

"One, two, three," they all counted. The nurse said, "All done!" Jake blinked. It was over that fast. "My arm was soft, so it hurt less," Jake said. The nurse smiled. "That's right. You did it yourself."

She put the duck bandage on his arm. Jake got the little fork prize too. At home, Jake used his new fork to feed himself dinner. He took one bite, then two bites, then three. "Mom, can we count my ice cream too?" he asked. Mom laughed and scooped a big bowl.

Dad said, "We can come back later. The bus comes at two o'clock." Athena waited by the door. She watched the big clock on the wall. The hands moved slow, slow, slow.

Then a box came off a truck. The lady opened it. Pink hats! New hats for today. "The truck brings new things," Athena said. "Yesterday the hats were gone. Now there are more." She picked the best pink hat.

The bus came at two o'clock. Athena held the hat box on her lap. "Tomorrow Grandma will smile," she said. Dad smiled too.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Rowan sat at the dinner table. He took a big bite of warm rice. His tummy felt happy.

Rowan had a problem. He wanted to play outside after dinner. "No outside," said Mama. "It is almost bedtime." Rowan looked down. Why did bedtime come so fast?

Then Rowan took a sip of warm milk. It felt warm in his tummy. He yawned a big yawn. Why was he so sleepy? He drank more milk. He yawned again. "Warm milk makes me sleepy," he said. The warm milk made his eyes blink slow.

After dinner, Mama ran a bath. The water was warm and bubbly. Rowan patted the bubbles with his hand. Pop, pop, pop! He patted them some more. The warm water made him feel even sleepier.

Mama helped him put on his soft pajamas. One sock, then the other sock. His feet were warm now. Rowan yawned one more yawn.

He did not go outside. He went to bed instead. "Warm milk, warm bath, warm socks," said Rowan. "All warm things. All sleepy things." He hugged his bear and closed his eyes. Outside could wait for morning.

story:
Ayla went to the park with her doll, Pip. Ayla wanted to play house. She found a big flat rock. "This is our house," she said.

Pip needed a bed. Ayla made a bed from leaves. The leaves were soft. The bed was cozy. But Pip had no blanket. Ayla looked around. She found a big green leaf. She put it on top. "Sleep now, Pip," she said. Pip lay very still.

Then Ayla wanted to feed Pip. She had no spoon. She looked down. She picked up a little stick. The stick was not a spoon. But she held it like a spoon. "Here comes food!" she said. She tapped the stick on a bottle cap. Tink, tink. "Pip, the stick is a spoon because we say it is!" Ayla laughed. Pip said nothing. Dolls are quiet like that.

Grandma sat on a bench nearby. "Is Pip eating well?" asked Grandma. Ayla nodded. "Yes. She ate three leaves." Then the big green leaf blew off the bed. The wind took it! "Oh no!" said Ayla. "Pip is cold because the wind took her blanket." She ran and got two leaves this time. She put one under and one on top. "Now you are cozy twice, Pip." Grandma clapped her hands. "Best house in the park," she said.

activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Asher stood at the school gate. His mama held his hand. The gate was big and green. Asher did not want to let go.

"You can wave to me," said Mama. "I will wave back." Asher let go of her hand. He waved. Mama waved back, big and wide. Then she stood by the fence and waited.

Asher had an apple in his bag. It came from the farm at home. His hands were slippery from the rain, so the apple slipped out. It rolled on the wet ground. It rolled right to a girl with red boots.

She picked it up. She looked at his name tag. Everyone at school had a name tag on their shirt today. "Here is your apple, Asher," she said. Asher looked down. His name was right there on his chest!

"You know my name," he said. "Yes," said the girl. "Your tag tells me." She pointed to her own tag. "I am Nia. Want to walk in together?"

Asher took his apple. He took Nina's hand too. He turned and gave Mama one more wave. Then the two friends walked through the big green gate.

"Nia!" called a small voice. A boy was crying by the wall. His tag had flipped over, so nobody could read his name.

Nia turned it right side up. "Hello, Tom," she said. Tom wiped his eyes and smiled. "Come with us," said Asher. "We all have names now."

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Charlie wanted the blue truck. But her cousin Sam had it. Sam pushed the truck. Vroom, vroom.

"Can I have a turn?" Charlie asked.

Sam held the truck tight. He shook his head. Charlie felt like crying. But then she had an idea.

"Sam, you take a turn. Then I take a turn," she said. "That is fair."

Sam thought. Then he smiled. "One, two, three," he counted. He pushed the truck. Then he gave it to Charlie. She pushed it. Vroom, vroom.

"Your turn is short," said Sam.

"Why is it short?" Charlie asked herself. She looked at the clock. "Because my turn is one minute. Then I leave the truck for you."

They took turns all morning. Soon it was lunch. Mom called, "Wash your hands first!" Charlie did. Sam did too. That was a rule at the table, and Mom said rules keep everyone safe and happy.

Sam put a carrot on Charlie's plate. "I share with you," he said. It looked funny sticking up like a little tree. Charlie laughed and took a big bite.

"More turns after lunch?" asked Charlie.

"Yes," said Sam. "You go first."

Her friend Ben showed her his card. "This is B," he said. "B has two bumps." Zoey looked hard. She turned her card. "My D has one bump," she said. "One bump, one bump," she said again. Now she could see it.

Miss Kim asked, "What sound does B make?" Ben said, "Buh, buh, bus!" Zoey clapped. She found a new B card. "Buh, buh, bear!" she said. Ben gave her a high five.

At play time, Zoey drew a beautiful sweater on paper. She made a big B on it. "B is for sweater bumps," she laughed. Then she drew fish. "They swim fast," she said. She looked at the word fish. "F! Fuh, fuh, fish!" said Zoey.

Charles held up his picture. "Look, it sticks now!" he said. The sparkles sat on the table. His shiny sun glowed in his hands.

"One square, two squares, three squares," he said. He glued the brown square on the paper. "The square is the house," he said. Now he needed a roof. He picked a circle. He put it on top. The circle wobbled and slid off. He put it on again. It slid off again.

Ibrahim picked up a triangle. It had three straight sides. He put it on top of the square. It sat flat and did not fall. "The circle fell because it was round," Ibrahim said. "The triangle stays because it is flat on the bottom."

His friend Maya yelled, "My roof fell too!" She held a circle in her hand. Ibrahim gave her a triangle. "Try this one," he said. She put it on her house. It stayed.

Then Maya gave Ibrahim a spoon. He used it to spread the glue. He pressed on one triangle, one square, one rectangle door, and one circle sun.

"Look at my house!" Ibrahim said.

Teacher Sam smiled. "Nice roof," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
John was at Grandma's house. He wanted to play outside. It was cold, so he had to wear his coat. "I can do it myself," John said.

He pushed his arms in the sleeves. Then he grabbed the zipper pull and pulled it up. But the zipper did not move. John pulled again. The zipper still did not move. "Silly zipper!" he said. Grandma laughed a little. "Try looking at the bottom," she said.

John looked down. There was a little metal pin sticking out at the bottom. The other side had a little slot. John pushed the pin into the slot. It clicked in. Then he pulled the zipper pull up. Zip! It went all the way to his chin. "The pin has to go in the hole first," John said. "That's why it was stuck!"

"Smart boy," said Grandma. They went outside to the garden. A frog sat by the pond. It made a loud jump into the water. Splash! "Take that, cold day!" said John, and he zipped his coat up even more.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Lena wanted to draw a cat at school. But the paper box was empty. No paper left.

Teacher Sam showed her the tablet. "Hold this button," he said. "Count one, two, three." Lena held the button. One, two, three. The screen grew bright. A yellow cat picture shone on it.

Lena tapped the drawing app. It was a little brush with rainbow colors. She drew a big yellow cat with long whiskers. Then Tom came over. He looked sad. His phone was dark, and he did not know why. "Hold the button and count," said Lena. Tom held it. One, two, three. His screen lit up too. "The button makes it wake up!" said Lena.

Then it was cleanup time. Lena pressed the top button. The screen went dark. She carried the tablet with two hands. She set it in its box, all tidy. Teacher Sam smiled. "You put it away so well," he said. Lena clapped her hands. "I can do it all by myself," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Paint day was here at last. Charlotte wanted to paint a green tree. But there was no green paint. There was red, yellow, and blue.

A boy named Sam sat next to her. "No green," he said. He helped her open the little paint cups. The school dog, Bingo, barked one happy bark at the smell of paint.

"What will make green?" Charlotte asked herself. She put yellow on her brush. Then she put blue on top. She mixed them on the paper. The paint turned green! "Yellow and blue make green," she said.

She painted a big green tree. Sam mixed red and yellow. His paint turned orange. He painted a fox. Charlotte hung her tree on the wall. "Look, green," she said, and smiled.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Jasper woke up in his bedroom. He wanted his blue sock. "I had it yesterday," he said. Yesterday was the day before today. The sock was not on his foot now.

Jasper looked under the bed. No sock. He looked on the rug. No sock. He looked in his toy box. No sock. "One bed, one rug, one box," he said. "Still no sock."

Mama came in. "I put your socks in the wash yesterday," she said. "Sorry, Jasper. The wash takes time. It is going now. It will be done later." Jasper put on his yellow socks today. "The blue socks come back later," he said. "Then I will wear them tomorrow." He kept his shoes by the door. Later could wait. Mama smiled and said, "Let's go eat."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Oliver sat at the camp craft table. He was making a paper lion. He wanted it for his grandma.

First he cut the mane. Then he cut the face. Now he needed to glue them together.

Oliver squeezed the glue bottle. Squeeze, squeeze, squeeze. A big puddle came out. The paper got wet and soft. It wrinkled up like a raisin.

"Oh no," said Oliver. "Why did my paper get bumpy?"

He looked at the glue bottle. Then he looked at the puddle. Too much glue made the paper soggy. That was why.

His friend Mia sat next to him. Her paper was flat and smooth. She used tiny dots of glue. One dot here. One dot there.

Oliver asked, "Can I try small dots too?"

"Yes," said Mia. She pushed the glue bottle toward him.

Oliver took a fresh paper lion face. He made one small dot. He made another small dot. He pressed the mane down. The paper stayed smooth.

Then he set his lion in the sun by the window. Soon the glue was dry. The lion felt firm and crisp.

The teacher came by. "What a big lion! Look, it has a curly tail."

Oliver turned the lion over. He had not glued a tail at all. But there one was, drawn in orange crayon. Mia had drawn it for him while he was not looking.

Oliver smiled. "My lion is done," he said. "And it is flat!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Brielle stood in the reading corner. The rug was soft under her toes. A shelf of books stood by the window.

"Today you get a library card," Mom said. Brielle put her hand in Mom's hand. They walked to the big desk. The lady typed on her computer. Then she gave Brielle a small card. It had Brielle's own name on it.

"Pick one book," said Mom. Brielle looked a long time. She picked a book about a red truck. "I want to keep it forever," she said.

"You can take it home," said the lady. "But you must bring it back." Brielle held the book tight. "Then someone else can read it too," said Mom.

At home, Brielle read the truck book three times. She put it by her bed. Each night she read it again.

Then the day came. Mom said, "It is time." Brielle carried the book back to the library. She gave it to the lady. The lady put it on the shelf.

Brielle looked at the shelf. A boy was reaching for the truck book. "He can read it now," Brielle said. "Because I brought it back."

Then she picked a new book about the moon. "This one," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Aiden ran to the park. The sun did shine on the slide. He felt so excited. His tummy jumped like a little hop.

Then Aiden saw a boy cry by the swing. The boy was sad. His ice cream had fallen down. It fell because the cone was too wobbly. "It fell," said the boy. Aiden looked at the ground. He saw the pink ice cream by his shoe.

Then a big dog ran up fast. The boy hid behind the bench. He was scared. But the dog just sniffed the ice cream and wagged his tail. The dog wanted the ice cream, not the boy. The boy came out from the bench. He laughed a little.

Aiden got mad one time too. A girl took the far swing, the one he liked. His face got hot. Then he took a big breath, like blowing out a candle. His hot feeling got small. The girl smiled and said, "You can have a turn next." Aiden felt happy inside. He watched the chickens peck far across the grass. "The dog came for the ice cream," Aiden said. "Not for us."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Matteo wants the cookies. Teacher Rosa hid them somewhere at daycare. "Can I find them?" he asks. "Yes, use your body," she says.

First he closes his eyes. He sees nothing. He opens his eyes. Now he sees the red shelf. "My eyes see the shelf. No cookies there."

Then he hears a sound. His ears hear it. Tap, tap. It is friend Mia with a spoon. No cookies there, either.

Matteo uses his nose. He sniffs near the big hill of blocks. Nothing. He sniffs near the toy box. Nothing. He sniffs by the little door. Mmm, sweet! "My nose smells cookies!" He follows his nose. The smell gets big. It leads him to the kitchen corner.

He touches the tin with his hands. It is warm. "Warm cookies!" He licks one crumb with his tongue. Sweet, so sweet.

The milk is hot, so he does not sip it. "Hot milk can burn my tongue," he says. He waits a short time. Then he sips. "Yum. My nose found them because cookies smell sweet!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Beatrice woke up on a sleepy morning at Grandma's house. She saw a big piano in the corner. Grandma smiled and said, "You can try it."

Beatrice sat on the bench. She touched one key very softly. The piano made a tiny sound. "Why so small?" she asked. She pressed the key again, this time with her whole hand. The sound grew big and warm. "I pressed hard, so it sings big," she said.

Grandma played one, two, three notes. Beatrice played one, two, three notes too. Then she tapped a key so gently that it made almost no sound at all. "I touched it light, so it sleeps," she said.

Then a small surprise came. Beatrice held down one key and tapped another. The first sound kept ringing, long after her finger flew away. She counted the rings in the quiet room. One, two, three, four. "The sound stays if I hold it," she whispered.

Grandma sat beside her. "Play with me," she said. Beatrice pressed the keys, soft and loud, loud and soft. Outside, a bird began to sing along. Beatrice laughed and played one more note.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Lily sat at Grandma's big table. She had a new pencil and empty paper. "I want to write my name," she said. But the pencil kept slipping. Her letters came out wiggly and wrong. Why did the pencil slip?

Lily held the pencil in her whole fist. That was the problem! She looked at Grandma's hand. Grandma pinched the pencil with two fingers, like picking up a tiny seed. Lily tried it. She pinched the pencil with her thumb and one finger. The pencil sat snug, like a little stick resting on a branch. It did not slip at all.

Lily wrote a big L. Then i, l, and y. "Lily!" she said. "That's me!" She drew a picture of her street next to it. Grandma clapped her hands.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Henri was awake early. Today was his first day of school. He put on his red shirt. He packed his toy car in his little bag. "You will find your name there," Mama said.

At school, Henri saw small doors on the wall. Each door had a name. He looked and looked. Then he saw a red triangle. His name was on the red triangle. He hung his bag under it. The toy car went in too.

A boy chased a ball near the toys. Henri chased it too. They laughed. The teacher looked at the red triangle. "Henri," she said, "your bag is safe there." Henri smiled. The door held his bag because it had his name. He waved to Mama. "My name stays here," he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Josephine went to the park with Grandma. She wanted to find the ducks by the pond. "Stay close to me," said Grandma. Josephine held Grandma's hand.

Near the pond, there was a small fire. A man was cooking on it. The fire was orange and jumpy. Was it hot or cold? Josephine wanted to poke it with a stick. She begged, "One little touch, Grandma?"

Grandma pulled her back. "No touching the fire," she said. Then she held Josephine's hand near the warm air above it. Not on it, just near it. "Ooh, warm," said Josephine. The fire made heat. Heat could hurt her skin.

A kind man by the fire gave her a warm bun instead. Josephine blew on it. She took a tiny bite. Yum.

Then she saw the ducks. She stayed close to Grandma all the way to the water. The fire is hot, she thought, so I don't touch it. The bun was warm, so she could eat it slow.

"I found the ducks, Grandma!" she said.
